sections.title: Train on a Mac (Apple Silicon)
sections.blurb: Everything here runs on a MacBook with 16 GB. This is what the Flisk model was trained with.

items.what: Fine-tune (LoRA, QLoRA, DoRA), fuse, quantize and serve LLMs on Apple Silicon. The tool behind the worked example below.
The array framework under it: NumPy-like, runs on the Mac GPU with unified memory.
Worked examples for MLX, from text generation to fine-tuning.
Apple's own toolkit for training small and large models, for language and vision.

sections.title: Fine-tuning libraries
sections.blurb: Pick one. They all do LoRA/QLoRA; they differ in speed, memory use and how much they hide.

items.what: Fast, low-memory LoRA training with free Colab and Kaggle notebooks.
The standard library for LoRA and other parameter-efficient methods.
Supervised fine-tuning plus preference methods (DPO and friends) on top of PEFT.
Config-file driven fine-tuning of many models, single GPU to multi-GPU.
A broad fine-tuning toolkit with a web UI, for many model families.
PyTorch-native, readable fine-tuning recipes.
Fine-tune models with a config file or a UI and little code.

sections.title: Run, quantize and serve
sections.blurb: Turning a trained model into something people can call.

items.what: Run models on CPU and GPU, convert to GGUF, quantize, and constrain output with grammars.
One-command local model server with an OpenAI-compatible API and a Modelfile format.
High-throughput GPU serving engine.

sections.title: Make the output valid
sections.blurb: For structured answers such as JSON or config files, force the output to match a schema instead of hoping.

items.what: Structured generation: constrain a model to a JSON schema, regex or grammar.
Fast constrained decoding engine used by several serving stacks.
Efficient grammar-constrained decoding for LLM serving.

sections.title: Test your model
sections.blurb: A model you cannot measure is a model you cannot improve.

items.what: The standard harness for benchmarking language models.
Lightweight evaluation toolkit from Hugging Face.

sections.title: More ways to evaluate
sections.blurb: Beyond the general harnesses above, these fit code and structured-output models.

items.what: Stricter evaluation of code-generation models.
A framework for evaluating code-generation language models.
Unit-test style evaluation for LLM applications.
Test and validate data and models, from research to production.
Load, share and process datasets of any size.
Build synthetic datasets and feedback pipelines for fine-tuning.

sections.title: Track experiments and version data
sections.blurb: Training runs are easy to lose. These keep a record of what you ran, on which data, with which result.

items.what: Track runs and metrics, package models, and keep a model registry.
Version datasets and models alongside your code, like git for data.
A fast, self-hosted experiment tracker with a good comparison UI.
Experiment tracking, orchestration and data management in one open-source suite.
Run training and report results from CI, so every pull request shows its metrics.
Git-like branches and commits for the data lake behind your training data.
Package a model, its data and code as one versioned, shareable artifact.

sections.title: Label and generate data
sections.blurb: Good data beats a bigger model. Tools for labelling, cleaning and synthesising it.

items.what: Collaborative labelling and feedback for LLM and NLP data.
A flexible open-source labelling tool for text, audio, images and more.
Find label errors and bad examples in a dataset automatically.
Scalable data curation: filter, deduplicate and prepare training data.
Generate realistic synthetic tabular data from a real dataset.

sections.title: Shrink and compress models
sections.blurb: Smaller models run on cheaper hardware. Quantization is the usual first step.

items.what: Activation-aware 4-bit quantization for LLMs.
Simple quantization for PyTorch and Transformers models.
The tensor library under llama.cpp, with its own quantization formats.
Quantization, pruning and distillation toolkit for many frameworks.
An open format for moving models between frameworks and runtimes.

sections.title: Serve in production
sections.blurb: Once a model works, put it behind a reliable API.

items.what: Package a model as a service and deploy it anywhere.
Run a large model across your own devices, Macs included.
An open-source way to provision cloud GPUs for training and serving, without being tied to one provider.

sections.title: Small open models with a clear licence
sections.blurb: Licence column is read from each model's own card. Check it before you sell anything built on a model.

items.what: Small coding model. Fine-tuned in the worked example below.
Larger coding sibling.
The middle size. Note its licence is different from the other two.
Small general model built for on-device use.
Small reasoning-leaning model from Microsoft.
The simplest, fastest repo for training and fine-tuning medium-sized GPTs.
Build a GPT-style model step by step, with code and explanations.

sections.title: Free compute
sections.blurb: Free tiers change often, so check the current limits before you plan around them.

items.name: Google Colab
items.what: Free notebooks with a GPU for short sessions. Many fine-tuning notebooks run here.

items.name: Kaggle Notebooks
items.what: Free GPU hours per week in the browser.

items.name: Hugging Face LLM course
items.what: A free course on transformers, fine-tuning and evaluation.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.blurb: A full small-model project with its numbers published, including the failures.

items.what: Trains a 1.5B model on a MacBook to write Flisk config files, graded by the real validator, with Claude, Qwen and prompted baselines.
A large curated list of open-source tools for production machine learning: serving, monitoring, data pipelines and more. Several entries above were found through it.
